title: Dracula
author: Bram Stoker
setting: Transylvania, Whitby, Purfleet, Hampstead and London, then the Danube and the Borgo Pass
lengthNote: Twenty-seven chapters and a closing note, with no narrator outside the documents
openingLine: 3 May. Bistritz.—Left Munich at 8:35 p.m., on 1st May, arriving at Vienna early next morning; should have arrived at 6:46, but train was an hour late.
summary: A solicitor’s clerk goes to Transylvania to complete a property purchase and finds his client is not leaving the country alone. Stoker tells the whole thing in journals, letters, telegrams, ships’ logs, newspaper cuttings and phonograph cylinders, so the reader assembles the danger months before the characters manage to compare notes. The hunt is finally won by filing: Mina types the papers into order, and the order shows them where he has gone.
referenceStyle: chapter, with the closing section given as Note

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Dracula
sourceText.note: Chapters are numbered but untitled in the original; the closing section is headed Note. Stoker’s characters date their entries by day and month and never give a year.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: In London by Archibald Constable and Company, in yellow cloth with red lettering.

atAGlance.label: Form
atAGlance.note: Journals in shorthand, letters, telegrams, a ship’s log, newspaper cuttings, a phonograph diary and a memorandum — no outside narrator at any point.

atAGlance.label: Research
atAGlance.note: Stoker’s working papers show the name and the Transylvanian setting arriving late, over an existing plan.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.value: Twenty-seven chapters and a closing note
atAGlance.note: Roughly four in the castle, ten in England, and the rest a chase back the way Harker came.

structure.label: Chapters I-IV
structure.title: A business trip that turns into an imprisonment
structure.summary: Harker records meals, train times and local customs with a clerk’s precision, and keeps recording them as the food becomes strange, the peasants press crucifixes on him and his host turns out to cast no reflection. The documentary habit is what makes the horror land: nothing is asserted, everything is minuted.

scenes.summary: The journey through Bistritz and the Borgo Pass; Dracula’s welcome at the threshold; the shaving mirror.
The Count’s history of his race, the crawling descent of the wall, and the three women in the unused room.
Fifty boxes of earth, the letters Harker is forced to post-date, and his climb down to escape.

structure.label: Chapters V-VIII
structure.title: Letters between two women, and a ship that arrives steering itself
structure.summary: The novel switches to Lucy and Mina’s correspondence, three proposals of marriage in one day, and a seaside holiday. Then a storm drives an empty Russian schooner onto the sands at Whitby with its dead captain lashed to the wheel, and a large dog leaps ashore. Lucy starts walking in her sleep.

scenes.summary: Lucy’s three proposals, Seward’s phonograph diary, Renfield’s ledger of flies and spiders, and the Whitby churchyard.
The cutting from the Dailygraph and the Demeter’s log, kept until the last crewman is gone.
Lucy found on the seat above the harbour with two small punctures; Mina is called to Budapest to marry Jonathan.

structure.label: Chapters IX-XIII
structure.title: Four transfusions and a funeral that does not hold
structure.summary: Seward cannot account for anaemia without blood loss and sends for his old teacher. Van Helsing knows at once, treats with garlic and transfusion, and is defeated four times by a household that keeps tidying the flowers away. Lucy dies, is buried, and children on Hampstead Heath begin coming home with small wounds.

scenes.summary: Van Helsing arrives; the first transfusions; the garlic that a well-meaning mother removes from the room.
The wolf Bersicker, Mrs Westenra’s death, and Lucy’s last change of voice at the moment of dying.
The funeral, the newspaper reports of the bloofer lady, and Van Helsing’s proposal to open the tomb.

structure.label: Chapters XIV-XVIII
structure.title: Mina types the papers, and a scattered case becomes one story
structure.summary: The novel’s real turning point is clerical. Mina transcribes Jonathan’s shorthand, copies Seward’s cylinders, and puts every document into one chronological sequence, at which point five people can finally see what the reader has seen since Whitby. Lucy is dealt with in her tomb, and the group agrees to hunt.

scenes.summary: Mina’s transcription; Van Helsing reads Jonathan’s journal; the tomb is found empty and then occupied.
The woman in the churchyard, the child she carries, and what is done at the tomb by daylight.
The papers are brought together at Purfleet; Van Helsing sets out what a vampire can and cannot do.

structure.label: Chapters XIX-XXIII
structure.title: Fifty boxes, one asylum window, and the price of leaving Mina out
structure.summary: The men decide to protect Mina by excluding her from the work, and the decision is what exposes her. Renfield is beaten to death for refusing an invitation; upstairs, the group breaks in on a scene that Seward describes and Mina afterwards has to live with. She is marked on the forehead by the communion wafer.

scenes.summary: Carfax is sterilised box by box; Mina is kept from the meetings and begins to sleep heavily.
Renfield’s confession and death; the scene in the Harkers’ bedroom; the burn on Mina’s forehead.
Piccadilly, the last box, and Dracula’s promise that his revenge has only started.

structure.label: Chapters XXIV-XXVII and the Note
structure.title: A chase by timetable, and a record nobody could produce in court
structure.summary: Mina’s hypnotic trances give the group a compass and her own condition gives them a clock. They work out the route by shipping schedules and river maps, split into parties, and reach the castle road as the sun goes down. The closing note, written seven years later, admits that not one of the papers is an original.

scenes.summary: Mina is hypnotised at dawn and dusk; the party divides for Varna and then Galatz.
The river journey, the horse-borne pursuit, and Van Helsing and Mina crossing the last miles alone.
The three women dealt with at the castle, the fight at the gate, Quincey’s death, and a postscript about proof.

characters.name: Count Dracula
characters.role: A Transylvanian boyar, and a purchaser of London property
characters.summary: He appears in person in perhaps a dozen scenes and is offstage for most of the book, which is why he works. He is a historian of his own family, a careful reader of Bradshaw and the Law List, and his invasion of England is carried out by conveyancing, shipping agents and carters.
characters.clue: He studies English from books until his accent is perfect, buys a ruined estate by post, and packs fifty boxes of his own soil for the journey.

characters.name: Jonathan Harker
characters.role: Newly qualified solicitor, the novel’s first narrator
characters.summary: He goes east to complete a purchase and keeps taking notes after the notes stop being professional — recipes, train times, then the fact that his host has no reflection. His shorthand journal is the document everything else is later measured against, and for four months nobody believes a word of it, including him.
characters.clue: He asks the waiter for a paprika recipe to send home, and carries on making entries in the same notebook while climbing down a castle wall.

characters.name: Mina Harker
characters.role: Assistant schoolmistress, then the hunt’s archivist
characters.summary: She learns shorthand and typewriting to be useful to her husband and ends up as the only person who can see the whole case, because she is the one who puts it in order. The men then decide to protect her by leaving her out, and every disaster in the second half follows from that decision.
characters.clue: She practises stenography to help her fiancé, and it is her chronological typescript, not anyone’s courage, that shows five men where the enemy has gone.

characters.name: Lucy Westenra
characters.role: Mina’s friend, engaged to Arthur Holmwood
characters.summary: She receives three proposals in one day and asks in a letter why a girl cannot marry three men. The novel then spends five chapters draining her, killing her, burying her and killing her again, and the second death is carried out by the man she was going to marry with the other two watching.
characters.clue: Three men propose to her on the same day, and all three of them give her their blood before the year is out.

relationships.label: proposed to by, and patient of

characters.name: Professor Abraham Van Helsing
characters.role: Dutch physician, lawyer and philosopher, Seward’s old teacher
characters.summary: He arrives with a diagnosis he refuses to state, which is both a medical judgement and a narrative device. His English is wrong in a consistent and characterised way, and his argument against his own profession — that science wants to explain everything and dismisses whatever it cannot — is the book’s defence of its own plot.
characters.clue: A Dutch doctor with several degrees and shaky English, who treats a wasting illness with garlic flowers and will not say why until he has been proved right.

characters.name: Dr John Seward
characters.role: Head of the asylum next to Carfax
characters.summary: He dictates his diary onto wax cylinders, which is both the most modern thing in the novel and the reason his account cannot be searched until Mina types it out. He is a careful clinician who keeps a man in a cell while failing entirely to hear what the man is telling him.
characters.clue: He records his private grief on phonograph cylinders, and does not notice that the lunatic in his care is announcing the neighbour’s arrival.

characters.name: R. M. Renfield
characters.summary: He eats flies, then feeds them to spiders, then the spiders to sparrows, and keeps a ledger of the lives he has accumulated. He is the only person in England who knows Dracula has arrived, and he is the only person nobody thinks to ask. He dies for refusing to let his master in a second time.
characters.clue: He keeps an account book of the flies, spiders and birds he has eaten, and is beaten to death for changing his mind about an invitation.

characters.name: Quincey Morris
characters.role: A Texan, one of Lucy’s three suitors
characters.summary: He talks in a stage American that even the other characters notice, proposes to Lucy with a speech about prairie fires, and is the only member of the party who reacts to a wolf in the grounds by buying Winchesters. He dies at the castle gate and the last child born to the group carries his name.
characters.clue: The one American in the party, who answers a supernatural threat by buying rifles, and whose name is given to the child born on the anniversary of his death.

themes.name: Blood and contagion
themes.summary: Blood in this novel is property, inheritance and infection at once. Dracula lectures Harker on the blood of his race before anyone has been bitten; Lucy receives blood from four men in one week; and the final horror at the Harkers’ bedside is a forced exchange rather than a theft. Nothing here stays inside one body.
themes.development: A boast about ancestry in Chapter III, a transfusion ward in Chapters IX to XII, and a scene in Chapter XXI that the novel’s own narrator can barely bring himself to write down.

themes.name: Modernity against the old world
themes.summary: Stoker arms his hunters with the newest equipment available in 1897: shorthand, a typewriter, a phonograph, telegrams, blood transfusion, Kodak photographs and railway timetables. The joke is that none of it detects anything. What finally works is the oldest office skill in the book, which is putting papers in date order.
themes.development: Harker’s shorthand in Chapter I, Seward’s cylinders in Chapter V, and Mina’s typescript in Chapter XIV, which converts a pile of private records into a usable case.

themes.name: Arrival and invasion
themes.summary: The threat enters England legally. A solicitor conveys the property, a shipping firm moves the cargo, and a carter delivers the boxes to Purfleet for a fee. Late-Victorian anxieties about what might come in through the docks are given a shape that is less an army than a change of address.
themes.development: A purchase completed in Chapter II, a ship that reaches Whitby in Chapter VII, and a chase in the last four chapters that simply reverses the route.

themes.name: Women, desire and protection
themes.summary: The novel separates its two women and treats them very differently. Lucy’s appetite is punished in a tomb; Mina is useful and is therefore shielded from the work, which is exactly how she is reached. The men’s protectiveness is presented as chivalry and shown, repeatedly, to be the tactical error that costs most.
themes.development: Lucy’s question about marrying three men, the three women in the castle, and the decision in Chapter XVIII to keep Mina out of the council.

themes.name: Faith, science and what counts as knowledge
themes.summary: Seward can only see a case of anaemia because anaemia is what his training allows. Van Helsing’s method is to keep an open mind past the point where his profession would close it, and to use a communion wafer and a garlic flower as instruments. The book sets belief and evidence against each other and then makes them cooperate.
themes.development: Lanyon-like scepticism in Chapters IX to XII, Van Helsing’s lecture on the limits of science in Chapter XIV, and his formal statement of the case in Chapter XVIII.

themes.name: Records, proof and the closing doubt
themes.summary: Everything the reader knows arrives as a document, and the last page points out that not one of those documents is an original. Seven years after the events the survivors hold a bundle of typescript that would convince nobody, and the novel’s final gesture is to refuse to ask for belief at all.
themes.development: Harker’s fear in Chapter IV that his journal will never be read, Mina’s transcriptions in the middle chapters, and the admission in the Note that there is hardly one authentic document among them.

techniques.name: Documentary form
techniques.definition: A narrative assembled entirely from papers, recordings and cuttings, with no outside narrator.
techniques.inThisBook: Journals, letters, telegrams, a ship’s log, a newspaper cutting, phonograph cylinders and a memorandum. Even the moment of the Count’s death is somebody’s diary entry written afterwards.

techniques.name: Multiple narrators
techniques.definition: Several first-person accounts, each limited to what that writer knew at the time.
techniques.inThisBook: Seven or eight hands write this novel, and their ignorance is the plot: Harker knows what the Demeter was carrying and cannot tell Seward, who is treating the result.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The reader knowing more than the characters, because of how the material is arranged.
techniques.inThisBook: Stoker prints the Demeter’s log immediately before Lucy’s sleepwalking, so a reader watches a diagnosis being missed for five chapters by people with all the information in separate drawers.

techniques.name: Idiolect
techniques.definition: Giving each character a distinct and consistent way of speaking.
techniques.inThisBook: Van Helsing’s broken syntax, Quincey’s Texan idiom, the Whitby fishermen’s Yorkshire and Renfield’s ledger-keeping precision make the documents identifiable before a heading names them.

techniques.name: Gothic setting
techniques.definition: Landscape and architecture used to generate dread and to trap characters.
techniques.inThisBook: Stoker puts the castle in the first quarter and then relocates the Gothic to a ruined Essex estate, a Hampstead tomb and a Piccadilly house with the dust sheets still on.

techniques.name: Inventory and catalogue
techniques.definition: Lists of objects, dates and quantities used to make the impossible feel administrative.
techniques.inThisBook: Fifty boxes counted and recounted, sailing dates, train timetables, Renfield’s tally of flies: the horror is tracked by arithmetic, and arithmetic is what eventually finds it.

quotations.text: Welcome to my house! Enter freely and of your own will!
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: The Count greets Harker at the castle door, standing perfectly still.
quotations.analysis: It sounds like hospitality and it is a legal condition: the folklore rule that a vampire must be invited is being satisfied in advance, and Harker signs up to it by walking through the door. The Count makes no move to meet him, which the text notes twice — the crossing has to be the guest’s own act.

quotations.text: Listen to them⁠—the children of the night. What music they make!
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: Wolves howling outside the castle during Harker’s first supper.
quotations.analysis: The possessive is doing quiet work — them, not the wolves — and the Count is watching his guest’s face to see whether the phrase registers. What follows is an apology for the tastes of a hunter, which is the second time in a page he has explained himself in terms that only make sense later.

quotations.text: I am all in a sea of wonders. I doubt; I fear; I think strange things, which I dare not confess to my own soul.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Harker
quotations.context: A journal entry written in the castle, before he understands he is a prisoner.
quotations.analysis: Three clauses, each shorter than the last, in a journal that has so far been full of train times and paprika. The diary is the only person he can talk to, and the last clause admits that he is censoring even that — the document the entire novel rests on is being written by a man who dare not write everything down.

quotations.text: We are in Transylvania; and Transylvania is not England. Our ways are not your ways, and there shall be to you many strange things.
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: Explaining away one of the household’s peculiarities to his guest.
quotations.analysis: He is telling the truth and using it as cover, which is his usual method. The sentence also states the book’s geography as a rule, so that the second half — in which the ways of Transylvania are unloaded at Whitby by a shipping agent — reads as a violation of terms the Count himself set out.

quotations.text: Blood is too precious a thing in these days of dishonourable peace; and the glories of the great races are as a tale that is told.
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: The end of the Count’s long account of his family’s wars.
quotations.analysis: He has spent several pages using blood to mean lineage, and here he prices it. The double sense is set up before a single drop is taken, so that every later transfusion carries an argument about descent as well as a medical procedure. A tale that is told is from the Psalms, and he means it as a complaint about being finished.

quotations.text: This man belongs to me! Beware how you meddle with him, or you’ll have to deal with me.
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: Driving the three women away from Harker in the disused room.
quotations.analysis: Harker has been lying still with his eyes almost shut, waiting, and his own journal admits to a wicked longing. The Count’s intervention is a rescue and a claim of ownership in the same sentence, and the vocabulary is commercial — belongs, deal — which is how he handles everything, including the Essex property.

quotations.text: The last I saw of Count Dracula was his kissing his hand to me; with a red light of triumph in his eyes, and with a smile that Judas in hell might be proud of.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Harker
quotations.context: Harker watches the Count leave the castle, having been made to write letters dated weeks in advance.
quotations.analysis: The triumph is over paperwork: the Count has just obtained three post-dated letters that will keep anyone from looking for Harker until long after he is dead. Stoker gives the villain his most theatrical exit in the novel at the exact moment his weapon is a set of forged dates.

quotations.text: God and the Blessed Virgin and the saints help a poor ignorant soul trying to do his duty.
quotations.speaker: The captain of the Demeter
quotations.context: The last entry in the ship’s log, found lashed to the wheel with the captain’s body.
quotations.analysis: The log is the purest example of the novel’s method: a form designed for positions, weather and watches, kept up by a man whose crew is vanishing one at a time. He records the facts he is permitted to record and can name nothing else, and the empty ship reaches Whitby carrying both its cargo and an official document that proves something happened without being able to say what.

quotations.text: The blood is the life! The blood is the life!
quotations.speaker: R. M. Renfield
quotations.context: Renfield, having cut Seward’s wrist and licked the floor, is taken away by the attendants.
quotations.analysis: He is quoting Deuteronomy, and Seward files it as a symptom. Every element of the diagnosis the doctors need is in this room — an appetite for blood, a servant who responds to a master, a man who knows the neighbouring house is occupied — and it is all written down under the heading of a case note.

quotations.text: There are darknesses in life, and there are lights; you are one of the lights.
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: Van Helsing to Mina, after reading her transcription of Jonathan’s journal.
quotations.analysis: He says it to the person who has just done the filing, not to anyone who has done anything brave, and it is worth setting beside the decision four chapters later to keep her out of the council. The novel praises Mina in the language of light and then removes her from the room where the work is done.

quotations.text: I shall get my typewriter this very hour and begin transcribing. Then we shall be ready for other eyes if required.
quotations.speaker: Mina Harker
quotations.context: Mina resolves to type out Jonathan’s shorthand journal.
quotations.analysis: This is the sentence on which the second half of the novel turns, and it is about office equipment. Ready for other eyes is the whole problem stated in five words: private records held by separate people cannot be compared, and a hunt that has failed for three hundred pages becomes possible the moment somebody makes copies.

quotations.text: Ah, it is the fault of our science that it wants to explain all; and if it explain not, then it says there is nothing to explain.
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: Rebuking Seward for refusing to believe what he has seen.
quotations.analysis: The broken grammar makes the argument sound folkloric, but it is a precise objection: a method that treats the unexplained as the non-existent will always return the answer it started with. Stoker gives his most modern characters the newest instruments in the world and then has the oldest man in the room point out that instruments only find what they are built to find.

quotations.text: the consensus of their excuses is that they had been with a “bloofer lady.”
quotations.context: A Westminster Gazette cutting about children going missing on Hampstead Heath.
quotations.analysis: The newspaper reports the phrase as a childish fashion and prints it in inverted commas to keep its distance. Bloofer is a small child’s attempt at beautiful, so the most frightening development in the novel reaches the reader as a piece of quaint local colour in a light news column — which is exactly how it reaches the characters.

quotations.text: She seemed like a nightmare of Lucy as she lay there; the pointed teeth, the bloodstained, voluptuous mouth⁠—which it made one shudder to see⁠—the whole carnal and unspiritual appearance, seeming like a devilish mockery of Lucy’s sweet purity.
quotations.speaker: Dr John Seward
quotations.context: In the Westenra tomb, before Arthur drives the stake.
quotations.analysis: Seward’s vocabulary gives the game away: voluptuous and carnal are not clinical terms, and the man writing is one of the suitors she refused. The novel keeps describing the changed Lucy in the language of unacceptable desire rather than of predation, which is why so much criticism has fixed on this scene.

quotations.text: you would in time, when you had died, have become nosferatu, as they call it in Eastern Europe, and would all time make more of those Un-Deads that so have fill us with horror.
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: Explaining to Arthur why Lucy’s kiss would have destroyed him.
quotations.analysis: The condition is described as an inheritance that spreads rather than as a curse on an individual, and the reasoning is epidemiological: one case makes more cases, indefinitely. Van Helsing borrows a foreign word to name it because English medicine has none, which is the novel’s argument about the limits of a vocabulary in one sentence.

quotations.text: There are such beings as vampires; some of us have evidence that they exist.
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: Opening the formal briefing at the asylum, with all the papers in order.
quotations.analysis: He states it as a finding rather than a revelation, and the second clause does the work: not belief, evidence, and some of us, meaning the people in this room who have read the typescript. The supernatural is admitted to the novel by the same procedure a court would use.

quotations.text: We have on our side power of combination⁠—a power denied to the vampire kind; we have sources of science; we are free to act and think; and the hours of the day and the night are ours equally.
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: Setting out the group’s advantages before the hunt begins.
quotations.analysis: Combination is a late-Victorian word for organised collective action, and it names the thing the novel actually values: not courage but committee work, shared papers and a division of labour. The Count is enormously strong and entirely alone, and the book’s proposition is that the second fact beats the first.

quotations.text: Unclean! Unclean! Even the Almighty shuns my polluted flesh! I must bear this mark of shame upon my forehead until the Judgment Day.
quotations.speaker: Mina Harker
quotations.context: After the communion wafer burns her forehead.
quotations.analysis: The cry is from Leviticus, where it is what a leper is required to shout to warn others off, and Mina applies it to herself before anyone else can. The novel has her take up the vocabulary of ritual pollution for something done to her while she was drugged and held down, and nobody in the room corrects her.

quotations.text: My revenge is just begun! I spread it over centuries, and time is on my side.
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: Cornered in the Piccadilly house, before escaping through the back.
quotations.analysis: It is the only speech he makes to the whole group, and the boast is about duration rather than strength. Everything the hunters have — telegrams, timetables, a chartered launch — is built for speed, and he answers with centuries. The last four chapters are the novel testing which of the two is right.

quotations.text: Now God be thanked that all has not been in vain! See! the snow is not more stainless than her forehead!
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: At the moment the Count crumbles, with Mina watching.
quotations.analysis: The victory is announced as a fact about a woman’s complexion. Van Helsing checks Mina’s forehead before he checks anything else, and the novel closes its plot by restoring her to a state of visible purity — which tells a reader a good deal about what was thought to have been lost.

quotations.text: We were struck with the fact, that in all the mass of material of which the record is composed, there is hardly one authentic document; nothing but a mass of typewriting
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Harker
quotations.context: Seven years later, taking the papers out of the safe.
quotations.analysis: The book’s last move is to withdraw its own evidence. Mina’s typing saved their lives by making the records comparable, and it destroyed them as proof by leaving no originals — the same act did both. A novel that has spent six hundred pages insisting on documentation ends by admitting it has none.

quotations.text: We want no proofs; we ask none to believe us!
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: The last speech in the novel, with the Harkers’ son on his knee.
quotations.analysis: He turns a fatal evidential weakness into a refusal, and then changes the subject to the boy’s mother. It is a generous ending and an evasive one, and it leaves the reader holding a book that has just declined to argue for its own truth.

timeline.label: Polidori’s The Vampyre is published
timeline.detail: Begun during the same 1816 Geneva summer as Frankenstein, and the story that made the vampire an aristocrat rather than a peasant revenant.

timeline.label: Bram Stoker is born in Dublin
timeline.detail: He was bedridden until about the age of seven, and later became an athlete at Trinity College.

timeline.label: Sheridan Le Fanu’s Carmilla appears in In a Glass Darkly
timeline.detail: A fellow Dubliner’s vampire novella, and the closest predecessor to Stoker’s handling of desire and illness.

timeline.label: Stoker becomes business manager of the Lyceum Theatre
timeline.detail: Twenty-seven years working for Henry Irving, whose stage presence is often heard behind the Count’s manners.

timeline.label: Stoker begins his working notes
timeline.detail: The surviving papers show a planned vampire novel taking shape before the name Dracula or the Transylvanian setting arrives.

timeline.label: A summer at Whitby
timeline.detail: The harbour, the abbey steps, the churchyard seat and the Russian schooner story all reached the novel from this visit.

timeline.label: Dracula published by Archibald Constable and Company
timeline.detail: A staged reading was given at the Lyceum in the same year, chiefly to secure the dramatic copyright.

timeline.label: Stoker dies in London
timeline.detail: He had written a dozen other novels, none of which is much read.

timeline.label: Murnau’s Nosferatu
timeline.detail: An unauthorised adaptation with the names changed; Stoker’s widow sued, and the court ordered the negatives destroyed.

timeline.label: Hamilton Deane’s authorised stage version opens
timeline.detail: At the Grand Theatre, Derby; the evening dress and the cloak with a standing collar are the play’s inventions, not the novel’s.

timeline.label: Universal’s Dracula with Bela Lugosi
timeline.detail: Adapted from the stage version rather than the book, and the reason most readers arrive expecting a very different Count.

places.name: Bistritz
places.note: Where Harker sleeps before the last stage, and where the landlady presses a crucifix on him.

places.name: The Borgo Pass
places.note: The road where the Count’s calèche takes over from the public coach, exactly at midnight.

places.name: Whitby
places.note: The harbour the Demeter runs into, and the churchyard seat where Lucy is found.

places.name: Purfleet
places.note: Carfax, the estate bought by post, with Seward’s asylum on the other side of the wall.

places.name: Hampstead
places.note: The Westenra tomb, and the Heath where children come home with small wounds.

places.name: Galatz
places.note: Where the box is transferred to a river launch, and the chase becomes a matter of maps and timetables.

criticalViews.position: A novel about invasion and the foreign
criticalViews.summary: The most established modern reading takes the Count’s careful, legal arrival — a purchase, a shipment, a change of address — as a late-Victorian anxiety about what might enter a confident empire through its own ports and offices.
criticalViews.counter: It can make the book tidier than it is. The Count’s most effective allies are English professionals doing their jobs properly, and the novel is at least as interested in them.

criticalViews.position: A novel about women and desire
criticalViews.summary: Criticism has long contrasted Lucy, whose appetite is punished in a tomb by the men who wanted her, with Mina, who is useful and is therefore shielded. The vocabulary Seward reaches for in the tomb scene is not medical, and the book’s own language keeps admitting it.
criticalViews.counter: Mina is also the most capable person in the novel, and the plot’s turning point is her clerical work rather than anyone’s heroism, which complicates any simple account of Stoker’s women.

criticalViews.summary: On this reading the subject is how a scattered group turns private records into shared knowledge. Nothing supernatural is defeated until the papers are copied and dated, and the closing note’s admission that no original survives is the book’s real last twist.
criticalViews.counter: The approach can leave the horror out. The scenes readers remember are in a tomb and a bedroom, not in a typing room.

criticalViews.position: The Count as a figure who barely appears
criticalViews.summary: Dracula speaks in only a handful of scenes and is absent from the middle of his own novel. Much of his power comes from being reconstructed out of other people’s documents, which is also why every adaptation has had to invent him.
criticalViews.counter: The absence may be a limitation rather than a design: Stoker’s notes show a good deal of material planned for the Count that never reached the page.

essayQuestions.question: What does Stoker gain by telling the whole novel in documents?
essayQuestions.focus: Form, dramatic irony and the closing note
plan: Establish the range: shorthand journal, letters, telegrams, a ship’s log, cuttings, phonograph cylinders and a memorandum.
Show how the arrangement creates irony — the Demeter’s log printed before anyone in England can read it.
Use Mina’s transcription in Chapter XIV as the hinge on which the plot turns.
Consider what the form costs: the Count can only be seen through people who fear or misunderstand him.
Close on the Note, where the survivors admit that not one of the papers is authentic.

essayQuestions.question: How does the novel treat Lucy and Mina differently, and why?
plan: Begin with Lucy’s letter about three proposals, and the novel’s response to the question she asks in it.
Trace the medical treatment of Lucy as a body acted on by four men in a week.
Read the tomb scene for its vocabulary rather than its events.
Set against it Mina’s usefulness, and the Chapter XVIII decision to exclude her from the council.
Ask whether the ending restores Mina or simply certifies her, and on whose authority.

essayQuestions.question: ’The most modern people in the novel are the least effective.’ Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Science, technology and Van Helsing’s method
plan: Inventory the modern equipment: shorthand, typewriter, phonograph, telegrams, transfusion, timetables.
Show Seward’s clinical training producing a diagnosis that cannot include the evidence.
Use Van Helsing’s objection in Chapter XIV about what science does with the unexplained.
Note that the decisive tools are in the end organisational rather than scientific.
Weigh the ending: the Count is destroyed by knives in the open air, after weeks of paperwork.

essayQuestions.question: How does Stoker create dread without showing very much?
essayQuestions.focus: Setting, absence and the Count’s brief appearances
plan: Count the scenes in which Dracula is actually present, and note how few they are.
Examine the castle chapters for the technique of accumulating small impossibilities in a factual register.
Use the Demeter’s log as the clearest case of horror generated by an official document’s limits.
Follow the Gothic as it moves from a castle to an Essex estate, a Hampstead tomb and a Piccadilly drawing room.
Conclude with the effect on adaptation: everything visual about the Count has had to come from outside the book.

discussionQuestions: Renfield tells the truth for several chapters and nobody listens. What would it have cost Seward to take him seriously?
Mina is excluded from the council in order to protect her, and the exclusion is what exposes her. Is the novel aware of this?
Dracula appears in very few scenes. Does that make him more frightening or simply thinner?
The last page says the papers would convince nobody. Why end a documentary novel by discrediting its own documents?
Almost every screen Dracula comes from the 1924 play rather than the book. What does the novel look like if you forget the cloak?

related.why: The other late-Victorian horror assembled from professional documents, and the other one in which respectable men decline to ask the obvious question.
The earlier novel built from letters and nested testimony, and the earlier monster who is described only by the people who fear him.
Collins’s method of narration by successive witnesses, which Stoker takes over almost intact and makes frightening.
The same documentary structure applied to a theft, and the source of the idea that each narrator should give evidence only within their own knowledge.
Published six years earlier, and the other 1890s novel about something in a locked room that must not be seen.
